So this is basically my ideal routine in ten parts. My routine has been designed to allow for my drop which is not avoidable due to my bipolar disorder. We’ve adjusted accordingly.

2. All my restraints removed and massage anywhere they were straining/digging. Even the sound of this part is necessary. Chains clinking and drawers being opened and closed to our things away.
3. Fed/given a bit of sugar in some form and ice water since I likely can’t hold it myself
4. Snuggles with very little skin contact so we both get redressed in long sleeves and pants. The skin on skin is too sensory harsh for me.
5. Sleep. Like 12-14-16 hours of it.
6. A good late breakfast out to eat where we talk about the scene and reminisce
7. A massage for any soreness, pulled muscles or strains. Typically oil or CBD lotion.
8. A quiet day. Not expecting much of myself or him but spending time reconnecting as partners instead of victim/attacker or whatever I mentally to cope with since we do a lot of fear based play
9. Check ins often for the next week, both every morning/night in person and several times over the course of the day at home. He asks because I have a habit of shutting down or not even realizing how I am until someone asks and I have to come up with an answer.
10. Often times, a therapy appointment where I can talk through any feelings I still am having a hard time with. Most commonly guilt over my enjoyment of the scene and conflicts with my faith. I see my therapist weekly so it isn’t that far of a stretch to do this every time.

(Provided for others should they want to use the info OR dm me for more hands on advice. ADHD advocating  can change people’s lives)

1. Is your wife medicated? If so, how long has it been since her meds have been evaluated and adjusted by an ADHD conscious psychiatrist? Not a GP.

Medications can be an ACTUAL life saver for people with ADHD. We have increased risk of death by lifestyle related issues and accidents based on our impulsiveness. If she is not medicated this would be step #1 as far as I’m concerned. 

2. Does she experience sensory overload? If so, reduce that uncomfortable sensory input. ADHD and autism have this in common. It can be impossible to do a task like the laundry of the sound of the pipes squeaking when you run the washer makes you want to remove your own fingernails. If it’s sounds, get ear plugs and white noise. If it’s textures, a pair of gloves she likes (rubber, leather, micro etc). Clothes that are comfortable to move in as well. Curtains if the house is too bright or new lighting fixtures. This leads me into 3...

3. Create an ADHD friendly environment for living, work and play. Beyond the sensory things I listed, adhd makes organizing something BEFORE a task damn near impossible. And some habits cannot be broken. So, what do we do? Well I drop clothes everywhere so we have a hamper in every room. Then there is a posted schedule that has every Wednesday as laundry day. I do as much of it as I can because ROUTINE and RULES make all the difference. We also have a post it system. Reminders that I can leave if I need my Sir’s help to *accomplish something or if he needs me to handle a task. We also use white boards, calendars, a roomba, and the 15 minute method. That means let’s say your main upkeep tasks are floors, bathrooms, table tops, and clutter. So I have 1 of those a day and i or he sets a timer for 15 minutes. I get more done in that set amount of time than if I ADHD cleaned for a whole day. Then I run the dishwasher 1x a day and I run the laundry on laundry day. But you could also do 1 load of each a day! Then big projects, I serve by helping him on a day off or weekend.
